abstract: The persistent progression and therapeutic resistance remain formidable challenges in the clinical management of malignancies. A pivotal mechanism underlying these clinical challenges is the formation of a tumor immune barrier at the tumor margin, which physically and functionally excludes immune cells from the tumor core. This barrier is primarily constructed by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), however, the precise mechanisms directing the reprogramming of resident normal fibroblasts (NFs) into these CAFs remain inadequately defined. In this study, we utilized spatial transcriptomics to confirm the presence of a CAF-rich immune barrier at the tumor margin of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). By performing integrated single-cell sequencing data analysis and functional assays, we identified osteopontin (SPP1) derived by OSCC cells as the predominant paracrine initiator of fibroblast reprogramming. Mechanistically, SPP1 binds the CD44 receptor on NFs to activate the PI3K/AKT/Twist signaling axis, which drives their transition into CAFs characterized by enhanced collagen production and increased invasive capacity. Notably, we demonstrated a self-reinforcing positive feedback loop wherein Twist activation upregulates CD44 expression, thereby amplifying fibroblast sensitivity to SPP1 and further sustaining the CAF phenotype. Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of any node within the SPP1/CD44/PI3K/Twist axis effectively attenuated the NF-to-CAF transformation and reduced collagen production. Our findings delineate an important molecular circuit underlying stromal remodeling in OSCC, the disruption of which can potentially prevent the CAF-driven immune barrier formation and overcome therapeutic resistance in OSCC.

summary: Tumor-derived SPP1 binds CD44 on fibroblasts, activating PI3K/AKT/Twist to convert them into CAFs that form an immune barrier in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
title: Tumor cell-derived SPP1 reprograms fibroblasts into CAFs via CD44/PI3K/AKT/Twist signaling axis to promote immune barrier formation in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
